body.statement: For every finite admissible design class, the certified Pareto frontier is exactly computable by finite enumeration, certified infeasibility pruning, and certified dominance pruning.  A candidate may be discarded without running its remaining certificate tasks whenever a proved upper envelope for all of its attainable objective coordinates is weakly dominated, with one strict coordinate, by the proved lower objective vector of an already certified candidate.  After all unpruned candidates terminate, pairwise comparison of their certified output vectors returns exactly \(\mathfrak P_{\mathrm{adm}}\).  No assumption in the frozen core guarantees a strict reduction from exhaustive evaluation in the worst case: all admissible candidates can remain feasible and mutually nondominated.
body.proof_tex:
Finiteness follows directly from the caps.  There are finitely many integers \(J\), finitely many matrices
\[
M\in\{0,\ldots,m_{\max}\}^{J\times K},
\]
finitely many nonempty grid subsets of the finite set
\(\mathcal Z_{\mathrm{cand}}\) of size at most \(L_{\max}\), finitely many allocations and well caps in the declared finite sets, and finitely many integer truncation, moment, Taylor, subdivision, and precision choices under \(\mathfrak b\).  The additional inequality
\(\mathfrak B(\Xi)\leq B_{\max}\) only removes candidates.  Thus
\(\mathfrak X_{\mathrm{adm}}=\{\Xi_1,\ldots,\Xi_N\}\) for some finite \(N\).

For a certified candidate define the maximization-oriented vector
\[
y(\Xi)=\bigl(
\underline\Gamma_{\mathcal T},
\underline\kappa_{\mathcal T},
\underline\Lambda_{\mathcal T},
\underline\mu_{\mathcal T},
-N_{\mathrm{req}},-w_{\mathrm{cert}},-\mathfrak B(\Xi)
\bigr). \tag{34}
\]
Write \(y\succeq y'\) when every coordinate is at least the corresponding coordinate of \(y'\), and \(y\succ_{\!P}y'\) when additionally one inequality is strict.  The following finite algorithm is explicit.

First order candidates lexicographically by their finite encodings.  Apply the exact syntax, rank, simplex, box, and arithmetic-cap tests.  Maintain the set \(C\) of completed certified candidates.  For an unfinished candidate \(x\), interval computations may maintain an upper envelope \(U(x)\) satisfying \(y(x)\preceq U(x)\) for every possible certified completion.  If some \(c\in C\) satisfies \(y(c)\succ_{\!P}U(x)\), discard \(x\).  This is sound because transitivity would give \(y(c)\succ_{\!P}y(x)\).  Otherwise run the remaining finite certificate tasks.  At termination remove from \(C\) every \(x\) for which another \(c\in C\) has \(y(c)\succ_{\!P}y(x)\).

The certificate soundness theorem proves every infeasibility decision and every coordinate bound used by this algorithm.  A discarded candidate cannot be Pareto maximal by the preceding inequality.  Every retained candidate is certified and is not dominated by any certified candidate, because all unpruned candidates have terminated and the final comparison is exhaustive over \(C\).  Conversely every certified nondominated candidate is neither infeasible nor soundly dominated, so it survives.  The output is therefore exactly \(\mathfrak P_{\mathrm{adm}}\).

The frozen assumptions impose no theorem forcing an untested candidate to be infeasible or dominated.  A literal witness to the absence of a uniform strict-subenumeration guarantee is any admissible instance whose candidate sets and caps leave a singleton \(\mathfrak X_{\mathrm{adm}}=\{\Xi\}\) with \(\mathfrak C(\Xi)=\mathtt{CERTIFIED}\): its frontier is \(\{\Xi\}\), so its sole candidate must survive the tests that establish certification.  More generally, pairwise incomparable certified vectors cannot be dominance-pruned.  Thus the pruning characterization is exact and often useful, but a worst-case need to evaluate every surviving candidate cannot be removed without an additional monotonicity or dominance theorem.
